made. First, the complications associated with artiﬁcial nutritional support vary but are reported to be responsible for less than 3–5% of
deaths. Second, the outcome is dependent not only on the type of disease but also on the stage of the disease (e.g., patients with
advanced HIV who start HPN are only expected to survive a few months, whereas patients with less-advanced disease are expected
to survive longer). Third, the outcome of patients receiving HPN and HETF for a variety of conditions is available from the British Arti-
ﬁcial Nutrition Survey (Table 6). For patients on HPN, overall mortality at 1 year is 13%, with 19% returning to oral feeding and the
majority continuing with HPN. Patients with Crohn disease often have a good prognosis (with 2.5% mortality and 38% returning to
oral feeding within 1 year). For patients on HETF, typically an older patient group, mortality is higher overall (36% at 1 year) and the
outcome varies according to age and condition. The outcome data for two common conditions in adults and children receiving HETF
are shown in Table 6.
